title: Hazel in a forest garden
subtitle: A coppiced shrub that provides nuts, poles, and a productive shrub-layer role.
excerpt: Hazel earns its place in a forest garden as a coppiced shrub producing nuts in autumn, flexible poles for staking and weaving, and a dappled canopy under which shade-tolerant plants thrive. It coppices on a five to seven year rotation.
sourceNotes: Cultivation and coppice rotation notes from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Hazel woodland ecology from Oliver Rackham, Woodlands (2006). UK hardiness and growing conditions widely documented in horticultural literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: The cycle of years between cutting a coppiced shrub or tree to the base and the next cutting. Hazel on a five to seven year rotation grows back to harvestable pole size within that period. Shorter rotations produce thinner poles; longer rotations produce thicker poles or nuts. The same stool (root system) can continue on this rotation indefinitely.

content.text: Hazel in a forest garden fills the shrub layer at 2 to 5 m when uncut. On a
of five to seven years, it produces a crop of useful poles each cycle and keeps the system in light. For nut production, leave it uncoppiced or coppice on a longer cycle.

Plant bare-root whips from November to March. Space at 3 to 5 m for free-growing nut production; 2 to 3 m for a coppiced rotation. Hazel tolerates any reasonable soil and partial shade. It produces nuts best in full sun on fertile soil. Plant two or more for cross-pollination.

Harvest nuts in September to October, once the husks turn yellow-brown. Hazelnuts are ready to harvest when they fall freely from the husks. Pick before the squirrels take them: the squirrels usually arrive a week or two before the nuts are fully ripe, so monitor the tree from late August. Dry harvested nuts in a warm, well-ventilated spot for two to three weeks before storing.

Cut hazel to 20 to 30 cm above the ground in late winter (February to March). It regrows from the stool with multiple straight shoots. After five to seven years, harvest the poles and cut again. The poles are useful for bean poles, pea sticks, fence hurdles, and basket weaving.
